b: John Bohlinger met up with Ty Tabor and dUg Pinnick of King’s X at City Winery in Nashville. Their rigs are streamlined—Tabor has never owned an overdrive pedal, Pinnick’s main bass has a single knob on it, and between them there’s one stompbox on the floor—but effective. Have a look at some quick highlights below, and tune into the new Rig Rundown for all the details.

Tabor’s number one is a 2007 Les Paul Classic, completely chambered. He owns standards, a custom, and a second classic, but calls this his favorite of all of them. He’d retired a ‘76 Les Paul Custom over back problems, which is what sent him hunting for lighter guitars in the first place. He also prefers how the chambered body sounds — his solid ones are too dark, where this one has more life in the high end and will give him P-90-ish tones if he rolls back a little. It’s otherwise as Gibson built it, apart from the Seymour Duncan JB and Jazz set he put in.

A Mexican Stratocaster with a JB Jr. in it and stock single-coils elsewhere, out for about six songs in the middle of the set and again for the encore. Tabor has owned several American Strats and says the Mexican necks feel perfect to him. Through the amp it sounds almost identical to the Les Paul—what it does differently is clean up as soon as he rolls the volume back. Strings are DR Hi-Beams, .009–.042; DR turned up at a show years ago, handed the band strings and left, and Tabor and Pinnick put them on for soundcheck and never went back.

Tabor runs a first-generation Orange Crush 120, at least ten years old now. He grew up on solid-state and the early King’s X sound was all Lab Series, so tube amps leave him feeling lost. Orange sent him everything they had when they first started talking, prototypes from London included, and none of it was right. He called to thank them and bow out, and they mentioned they had one amp left—a transistor amp. It turned out to be the one.

Pinnick’s main bass is a Schecter semi-hollow, a model the company already made; when they offered him a signature and asked what he wanted, he said nothing pointy, and picked the one he did because he likes things understated. The first one came with two “fat” pickups he didn’t like the tone of and three knobs. They cut it to two, and then he asked for a single volume. The pickups now are a Seymour Duncan set the company discontinued years ago and makes only for him.

Around 1988, on one of King’s X’s first tours, Pinnick was standing next to Tom Petersson as Cheap Trick waited to walk onstage and told him the 12-string was crazy. Petersson handed it over. Pinnick is left-handed, so he turned it upside down, played a few notes, and was told to call Hamer. Each course runs one low string with two above it in octaves. He used to play it half the night and end up in real pain; these days it’s on four songs.

Pinnick goes into a tuner that stays on all night, there so he can glance down if he hears a wobble, and then into his signature dUg Tech 21 DP-3X, which has a tuner of its own and is where he actually tunes. Tech 21 came to him asking whether they could get his tone in a box, and what they landed on is decades of him EQing around the kick drum and the guitar so the bass stays huge without burying anyone. He sets it and leaves it, running everything wide open.

From the pedal, Pinnick runs into a Seymour Duncan PowerStage, going in the front because he likes to tweak the amp onstage even though front of house is taking a direct and blending the two. Behind him are four cabs with four 10s each, backs closed. They shipped ported, but he uses enough low end that the speakers would pop, and sealing them pushes the bottom. Tech 21 sent the grills.
